params.wrong_if: Contact centre records do not show ~38,000/month payee-setup calls at ~£280k monthly cost, or the one-in-five abandonment and subsequent salary-account attrition are not observed in the data

text: Filed as a business-level decision. The answer names the affected population (38,000 customers/month), frequency (monthly, Monday queue breach), and cost (£280k/month, £7.40/call, 11 minutes), plus a named downstream consequence (salary-account attrition) and a named source (app store reviews) — it has the shape the question asks for.

params.wrong_if: Records show the phone/branch process does not run the described identity checks and first-payment flow, or the annual cost is not around £3.4m, or branch/contact-centre hours differ from stated

text: Filed as a business-level decision, sibling to seq 3. The answer names the current channel (phone/branch), the actual steps performed, a named strength (fraud-spotting by a trained agent), and quantified shortcomings — hours of availability, £3.4m annual cost, and the strategic embarrassment given the app-first pitch.

params.wrong_if: Call recordings or logs do not show the re-reading of details, the close-match explanation step, the balance check before first payment, or the agent-initiated refusals for coached customers, or the one-in-twenty retry and ~300-a-year refusal figures do not hold up against records

text: Filed as a stakeholder-level decision under seq 4. The walkthrough goes past the documented script — the agent re-reading details, the close-match/sole-trader wrinkle, the balance check before first payment, and the undocumented coaching-detection step — each with a named frequency (one retry in twenty, ~300 stopped payments a year), which is what distinguishes it from the quality-manual diagram.

params.wrong_if: The payee-creation API cannot be called from the app channel with equivalent controls, or customers cannot resolve a non-match Confirmation of Payee result unaided, or the app-based fraud check catches scams at a lower rate than the phone agent does

text: Filed as a solution-level decision under seq 6. Each condition is a genuine bet, not a given: the API's app-channel callability, unaided customer resolution of non-match results, and the replacement fraud check matching the phone agent's catch rate are all things that could turn out false.

params.wrong_if: Post-launch fraud loss on app-created payees does not rise relative to the phone-handled baseline, or indemnity recovery on scammed Faster Payments is materially better than "pennies in the pound"

text: Filed as a solution-level decision, sibling to seq 7. The answer names three conditions, then singles out one — fraud control without a human in the loop — and backs the choice with a mechanism (Faster Payments' irrevocability, indemnity recovery at pennies in the pound) rather than just asserting it's the scariest one.

params.wrong_if: The build budget does not in fact sit with the Head of Payments, the operational saving is not booked against a different Operations director's plan, or the fraud team cannot in practice halt the rollout on rising losses

text: Filed as a stakeholder-level decision under seq 3. The answer names three distinct parties with three distinct stakes — the customer and contact centre who feel the pain, the Head of Payments who funds the build, the Operations director who books the saving, and a fraud-team veto that sits outside both budgets — which is the "at least three people" shape the question is after, not a single persona.

params.wrong_if: The work ends up scoped as a bolt-on quick fix rather than a full cycle, or delivery requires redesigning the existing pay flow rather than fitting inside it

text: Filed as a transition-level decision under seq 7. This names an appetite, not an estimate — full cycle, justified by two prior quick fixes that only moved the queue rather than fixing anything, with an explicit boundary that it must sit inside the existing pay flow rather than trigger a wider redesign.

params.wrong_if: The desktop-equivalent session controls turn out to transfer to the app without a gap, or a first-payment limit for new payees is not settled before build starts and rework follows, or the coached-customer warning design turns out to already exist off the shelf

text: Filed as a transition-level decision under seq 8. Each part of the question gets a specific answer rather than a deferral: named new technical work, a named unchecked assumption about control parity, a named unsolved design problem (the industry hasn't cracked it either), and a named decision — the new-payee payment limit — flagged as needing to be settled before the cycle starts rather than discovered mid-build.

params.wrong_if: The delivered first release includes any of international/non-sterling payments, business accounts, standing orders or Direct Debits, scheduled or bulk payments, Open-Banking-initiated payments, payee editing/deletion, under-16 customers, or identity/login control changes

text: Filed as a transition-level decision under seq 7. This names specific exclusions rather than leaving scope to be cut later, and closes with a one-line positive definition of what's in — a personal customer, in-app, a new UK sort code and account number, once, now — which pins the boundary from both sides.

params.name: PSR APP scam reimbursement rules / FCA Consumer Duty

params.wrong_if: Meridian's reimbursement liability, the sending/receiving bank split, or the £2.1m gross figure do not match actual claims data, or fraud operations do not in practice own APP claims while the journey owner and board are not the escalation points for Consumer Duty outcomes

text: Filed as a stakeholder-level decision under seq 3. This names the accountable parties at each layer — fraud operations for claims, the journey owner, the board under Consumer Duty — backs the cost with a figure (£2.1m gross last year) and a named regulatory mechanism (the effective-warning defence), and directly answers the second half of the question: removing the agent removes the shared liability that exists today.

params.wrong_if: Pilot data crosses one of the named thresholds — elevated scam-loss rate, a cap-breaching single loss, sub-70% completion, or above-average complaints — and the affected segment is not rolled back to the phone journey

text: Filed as a transition-level decision under seq 8. Each stop condition is a measurable, occurring result — a loss-rate comparison against a stated baseline, a specific cap-breach, a completion-rate threshold, a complaint-rate comparison — paired with a named consequence (rollback to phone for that segment), not a hypothetical that could never actually be observed.

params.wrong_if: Scam-loss and completion figures are not in fact tracked against the whole pilot population of new-payee attempts, the 85% first-attempt completion or no-worse-than-phone-baseline thresholds are not what determines pass/fail, or the two metrics are not reviewed weekly by fraud operations and the journey owner together

text: Filed as a transition-level decision under seq 8. Two named metrics with named owners, explicit pass thresholds, an exhaustive rather than sampled set, and a stated review cadence — this answers all four parts of the question rather than substituting a vibe-check or an off-domain benchmark.

params.wrong_if: Customers do not in fact self-explain the Confirmation of Payee result without help, the platform team cannot deliver the intervention and evidence pieces within a quarter, or fraud operations' and Operations' positions turn out not to be the deciding factor if scam numbers move

text: Filed as a solution-level decision under seq 9. All four risks are addressed by name rather than three of four: value (already the top complaint, driving second-account attrition), usability (flagged as the genuinely unproven one), feasibility (named components, named team, named timeframe), and business viability — fraud operations' nervousness and Operations' stake in the saving, with the political consequence named plainly rather than smoothed over.

params.wrong_if: Payee or customer data is processed or stored outside the stated UK data centres/cloud region, a processor beyond Pay.UK's name-check service touches the data (including any model or analytics vendor behind the scam intervention), or the existing privacy notice does not in fact cover this specific in-app flow

text: Filed as a solution-level decision under seq 14. This names the region, the one external party the data touches (Pay.UK's name-check service, stated as exhaustive), and the disclosure route (the existing privacy notice, carried over because the path matches the phone journey) — a region name backed by a sub-processor answer, not left bare.

params.wrong_if: The release ships without a first-payment limit, allows a customer to skip the Confirmation of Payee check, blocks a customer from paying after a no-match result, or quietly extends to international or business payments

text: Filed as a transition-level decision under seq 7. This names the regulated edge case directly rather than deferring it — the no-match result, where the answer states the refusal it will not make (blocking the customer's own money) alongside the ones it will (no skipping the check, a day-one payment limit, no international or business scope) — which is exactly the "regulated case as the edge case" the note warns against dodging.

params.wrong_if: The pilot is expanded beyond the stated 20,000 customers before the app's own scam-catch performance is measured, or the case rests on the phone team's 300 refusals and industry reports rather than evidence gathered from the app journey itself

text: Filed as a transition-level decision under seq 8. This names distinct evidence types for two separate claims — twelve months of contact-centre data, a 200-call listening sample, and twelve customer interviews for cost and demand, against only the phone team's 300 refusals and industry reports for the scam-replacement question — and draws the honest conclusion that the second is under-evidenced relative to its consequence, which is why the pilot is capped rather than universal.

params.wrong_if: The Confirmation of Payee check exceeds two seconds at the 95th percentile in production, or the median four-year-old-Android-on-4G-outside-London customer takes longer than three minutes from entering details to payment sent

text: Filed as a solution-level decision under seq 6. This names the slowest acceptable interaction and its percentile (name check, two seconds, p95), the whole-journey budget with device and network specified (a four-year-old Android on 4G outside London, under three minutes at the median), and an honest statement of today's baseline — nothing measured yet, against an eleven-minute phone journey that sets a low bar.

params.wrong_if: An hour of downtime does not in fact generate roughly 1,500 diverted calls or abandoned payments, a two-hour outage is not treated as a reportable event under operational resilience tolerances, or the payments platform team is not the one paged with escalation to the journey owner at thirty minutes

text: Filed as a solution-level decision under seq 14. All three parts are answered with specifics rather than a bare percentage: the expectation is anchored to a named peak moment (Friday evening, ~1,500 attempts/hour, and 11pm Sunday reflectiveness), the cost of an hour down is quantified in diverted calls and complaints with a two-hour regulatory threshold, and the paging chain names a team and an escalation time.

params.wrong_if: Launch proceeds without a completed audit from the external accessibility partner and sign-off from the digital accessibility lead, or testing does not in fact cover VoiceOver, TalkBack, switch access, 200% text, and the disabled customer panel

text: Filed as a solution-level decision under seq 9. This names the conformance level (WCAG 2.2 AA, matched to the rest of the app), the specific assistive technologies and conditions tested (VoiceOver, TalkBack, switch access, 200% text, plus a disabled customer panel), and a named checker with a named gate (external audit, digital accessibility lead sign-off, before launch rather than after) — level, technologies, and name all present.

params.wrong_if: The build stores the full name-check name beyond the match outcome, retains a screenshot or recording of the journey, keeps more than the customer's response to a warning, or data crosses the session boundary to a destination other than the name-check service and the payments platform

text: Filed as a solution-level decision under seq 14. The boundary is named (the authenticated session), what's allowed to cross it is enumerated rather than gestured at, the attacker model is specific and dual (the real-time phone coach, and account takeover) rather than generic, and the refusal-to-store list names three concrete things rather than invoking "encryption" as a stand-in for a boundary.
